newsitem.title: CANADA: Avenor shareholders reject Repap merger.
newsitem.headline: Avenor shareholders reject Repap merger.

text.p: Shareholders of Avenor Inc. on Wednesday rejected the Canadian pulp and paper concern's controversial C$2.6 billion ($1.9 billion) merger offer for Repap Enterprises Inc., leaving Repap's future in doubt.
At a special meeting, Avenor shareholders voted 74 percent against the proposal, which was pared down from a previous bid. Repap shareholders approved the deal at a separate meeting.
The rejection came just two days after Montreal-based Avenor said it turned down a friendly overture by Canadian paper maker Domtar Inc. to merge with Avenor and Repap.
Montreal-based Repap said it would pursue its options in light of the rebuff by Avenor shareholders.
"We will advise our shareholders of our alternative plans during the course of next week," Repap Chief Executive George Petty said in a statement.
Repap shares were down C70 cents to C$1.55 in active trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange after the vote. Avenor rose C60 cents to C$23.70 in Toronto and Domtar was down C45 cents to C$11.
On Tuesday, Finnish forest industry group UPM-Kymmene OY said it had prevously bid for parts of Repap.
Avenor Chief Executive Paul Gagne said he was disappointed with shareholder rejection of the merger offer and that the company was not pursuing talks with Domtar or Repap "at this time."
"We have got to respect the vote of the shareholders this morning. They said no to a transaction between Avenor and Repap," Gagne told a news conference after the vote.
But Domtar said it was still interested in a merger among it, Avenor and Repap.
"We were and we remain interested in putting the three companies together. We still think it is a good idea," Domtar spokesman Denis Couture said.
Avenor's bid for Repap ran into trouble earlier this week when Canada's largest pension fund, which holds 10 percent of Avenor, gave the deal a thumbs down.

Quebec's public pension and insurance fund manager Caisse de depot et placement said it was unhappy with the C$3.2 billion ($2.3 billion) of debt the merged entity would carry, and suggested that other institutions thought the same.

Gagne said Avenor shareholders appeared worried about the debt level of the proposed merged company and the interest costs it would face. They may also have been spooked by Tuesday's hike in U.S. interest rates, perhaps believing it to be a sign of higher rates to come, he said.
Avenor earlier this month cut its stock and debt offer to one Avenor share for every eight Repap shares and excluded Repap's British Columbia operations from the deal.
The original bid was one Avenor share for every 4.25 Repap shares, plus the assumption of Repap's debt.

Domtar is Canada's largest producer of fine papers. The Quebec government holds a 46 percent stake in the company through the Caisse and another agency. Repap is Canada's biggest coated paper maker and Avenor produces newsprint, pulp and white papers.

Repap is struggling with a C$2.4 billion ($1.75 billion) debt load and deep losses. It had a 1996 net loss of C$496 million ($362 million) against a profit of C$140 million ($102 million) in 1995. Net sales in 1996 were C$1.7 billion ($1.2 billion), down 17 percent from the year earlier.

Gagne said Avenor still considered newsprint its core business and would focus on improving margins at its existing operations. It planned to proceed with plans to divest its 53 percent stake in Pacific Forest Products Ltd. and its Gold River pulp mill in the west coast province of British Columbia.
